pathophysiology.summary: Anaemia affects more than half of Indian children and women. Iron deficiency is the main cause, from low dietary iron and bioavailability, blood loss (hookworm, heavy menstruation) and high requirements during growth, adolescence and lactation. Without iron, red cell production falls and cells become small and pale; low haemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery, causing fatigue, poor school and work performance, impaired cognitive development in children and increased risk in later pregnancy. Anemia Mukt Bharat combines prophylactic iron–folic acid (IFA) by life stage, biannual deworming, digital haemoglobinometer testing and treatment protocols with defined retest intervals. Grading uses WHO 2024 age-specific cut-offs. A rise of less than 1 g/dL after 1 month of good compliance is non-response, which needs referral and exclusion of haemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia), infections (malaria, TB, HIV) and chronic disease before more iron is given.
keyMechanisms: Inadequate intake and blood loss deplete iron stores.
Iron-restricted erythropoiesis causes microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
Hookworm and heavy menstrual loss add chronic blood loss.
Haemoglobinopathies mimic iron deficiency, and empirical iron can cause overload.

pathophysiology.summary: Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobinopathy in which a single beta-globin mutation produces haemoglobin S. In India it is concentrated in tribal populations of central, western and southern states, affecting about 1 in 86 tribal births, and the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission aims to screen and manage it. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises, deforming red cells into rigid sickles that haemolyse (anaemia, jaundice, gallstones) and block small vessels (vaso-occlusion), causing painful crises, acute chest syndrome, stroke, priapism, splenic sequestration and progressive organ damage. Early splenic dysfunction makes children vulnerable to severe pneumococcal and other infections. Crises are triggered by fever, dehydration, cold, exertion, surgery and infection. Hydroxyurea raises fetal haemoglobin and reduces crises; penicillin prophylaxis, folic acid and vaccination prevent complications; early aggressive treatment of pain and fever and referral for red-flag features save lives.

Haemolysis causes anaemia and jaundice.
Vaso-occlusion causes pain crises, chest syndrome, stroke and organ damage.
Functional asplenia increases severe infection risk; hydroxyurea raises HbF.

pathophysiology.summary: Beta-thalassaemia major results from inherited mutations that abolish or severely reduce beta-globin synthesis. India has one of the largest numbers of affected children worldwide. Unpaired alpha chains precipitate in red cell precursors, causing ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis; severe anaemia drives marrow expansion (bone deformities), extramedullary haematopoiesis and splenomegaly, and increased iron absorption. Regular red cell transfusion from early childhood corrects anaemia and suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, but each unit adds iron that the body cannot excrete, so iron accumulates in liver, heart and endocrine glands, causing cardiomyopathy, diabetes, hypogonadism and death unless chelated. Care therefore pairs transfusion to keep pre-transfusion haemoglobin at 9.5–10.5 g/dL every 2–5 weeks with safe, leucodepleted, matched blood, and chelation starting once ferritin reaches about 1,000 µg/L (usually after 10–20 transfusions), with regular toxicity and iron monitoring. Stem cell transplant is curative for selected patients.

Severe anaemia drives marrow expansion and extramedullary haematopoiesis.
Transfusion iron accumulates in liver, heart and endocrine organs.
Chelators bind iron for excretion but have dose-related toxicity.

pathophysiology.summary: India carries one of the world's highest burdens of oral cancer, driven by smokeless tobacco (gutkha, khaini, zarda, paan with tobacco), areca nut, smoking and alcohol. About a quarter of Indian adults use smokeless tobacco. Carcinogens such as tobacco-specific nitrosamines and chronic mucosal trauma cause stepwise changes from potentially malignant disorders (white or red patches, submucous fibrosis) to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, often presenting late. pathophysiology.summary: Alcohol-associated hepatitis is an acute inflammatory liver injury in people with prolonged heavy drinking, rising in India with increasing alcohol consumption. Alcohol metabolites, gut-derived endotoxin and oxidative stress activate inflammatory pathways and neutrophil infiltration, causing hepatocyte injury, cholestasis and impaired regeneration on a background of fatty liver or cirrhosis. Patients present with recent-onset jaundice (within 8 weeks), tender hepatomegaly, fever and features of liver failure; transaminases are only moderately raised (both under 400 IU/L) with AST/ALT above 1.5. Severe disease (modified Maddrey discriminant function 32 or more, or MELD above 20) carries about 50% short-term mortality. Prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days is used for severe disease without contraindications, and the Lille score at day 7 identifies non-responders (above 0.45) in whom steroids should stop. Abstinence is the single most important determinant of survival, alongside nutrition, withdrawal management and treatment of infection and complications.

Hepatocyte injury and cholestasis cause jaundice and coagulopathy.
Impaired regeneration leads to liver failure and high short-term mortality.
Corticosteroids suppress inflammation but raise infection risk.

pathophysiology.summary: Chronic heavy alcohol use down-regulates inhibitory GABA receptors and up-regulates excitatory glutamate (NMDA) activity. When intake stops or falls, this produces a hyperexcitable state: tremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, insomnia and restlessness, progressing in some to withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens, which can be fatal. Thiamine deficiency from poor nutrition puts drinkers at risk of Wernicke encephalopathy, which can be precipitated by glucose without thiamine. In India, alcohol use disorders are common and often present to general hospitals. Management uses a long-acting benzodiazepine (diazepam) titrated to symptoms and then tapered over 7–10 days, with lorazepam preferred in significant liver dysfunction, plus thiamine. Patients with previous seizures or delirium tremens, major medical or psychiatric comorbidity or failed outpatient treatment are admitted. Withdrawal care is the start of treatment for alcohol use disorder, followed by brief intervention, counselling and relapse prevention.

Abrupt cessation produces autonomic and neuronal hyperexcitability.
Severe withdrawal causes seizures and delirium tremens.

pathophysiology.summary: Heat stroke is a life-threatening failure of thermoregulation, increasingly common in India during heatwaves. When heat gain from the environment or exertion exceeds the body's capacity to lose heat, core temperature rises to 40 °C or more, causing direct cellular injury, a systemic inflammatory response, endothelial damage and coagulopathy. The brain is especially vulnerable, so central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, seizures, coma) defines heat stroke and separates it from heat exhaustion. Exertional heat stroke affects young labourers, soldiers and athletes; classic heat stroke affects the elderly, children and people with chronic illness during heatwaves. Multi-organ failure — kidney and liver injury, rhabdomyolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, electrolyte disorders — follows, with mortality of 40–64%. Outcome depends on how fast the temperature is brought down, so cooling starts at the scene and continues during transport, using cold-water immersion (gold standard for exertional cases) or evaporative cooling, monitored by rectal temperature, until it falls below 39 °C. Antipyretics do not work.

Central nervous system dysfunction defines heat stroke.

pathophysiology.summary: Arsenicosis is chronic poisoning from drinking groundwater containing inorganic arsenic, a major problem in the Indo-Gangetic and Brahmaputra plains (West Bengal, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Jharkhand). Arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and disrupts cellular enzymes and DNA repair. After years of exposure (pigmentation usually first, then keratosis over roughly 6–9 years), it causes characteristic skin changes: rain-drop melanosis or leukomelanosis on the trunk, and thickened keratoses on palms and soles. Systemic effects include peripheral neuropathy, non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis, chronic lung disease, peripheral vascular disease, anaemia, and skin (Bowen's disease, squamous and basal cell carcinoma) and internal cancers. There is no specific antidote in the national guidance; the core intervention is switching to arsenic-safe water, with nutrition, keratolytic ointments for keratosis, and surveillance for cancer and organ complications.

Chronic exposure causes pigmentation changes and keratinocyte proliferation.
Arsenic impairs DNA repair, causing skin and internal cancers.
Vascular, hepatic and neural toxicity cause systemic disease.

pathophysiology.summary: Fluorosis results from long-term intake of excess fluoride, mainly from groundwater, and affects many districts across Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and other states. Fluoride deposits in mineralising teeth and bone. In children, excess fluoride during tooth development causes dental fluorosis: white, yellow, brown or black horizontal streaks and, at higher levels, brittle chipped enamel, which is irreversible. In bone, fluoride increases density but reduces quality, causing osteosclerosis, ligament and interosseous membrane calcification, exostoses and, eventually, stiff neck and spine, inability to squat, deformities and crippling. Non-skeletal effects include gastrointestinal upset, anaemia, neurological symptoms and endocrine effects. Diagnosis combines water fluoride above 1.5 mg/L, urine fluoride and forearm X-ray. There is no drug cure; switching to safe low-fluoride water and a diet rich in calcium, vitamins C and E and antioxidants can reverse early deformities in children, while established adult deformities need surgery and rehabilitation.

Fluoride alters bone remodelling, causing osteosclerosis with poor-quality bone.
Ligament and interosseous membrane calcification causes stiffness and deformity.

pathophysiology.summary: Silicosis is an irreversible fibrotic lung disease caused by inhaling respirable crystalline silica dust in quarrying, stone cutting and crushing, mining, foundries, ceramics, cement and construction — industries employing millions of Indian workers, many informally. Silica particles are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, which are damaged and release inflammatory and fibrogenic mediators, forming silicotic nodules that coalesce into progressive massive fibrosis with restrictive lung impairment and respiratory failure. Silica-damaged macrophages also fail to control Mycobacterium tuberculosis, so silica exposure — and silicosis especially — greatly increases TB risk and worsens TB outcomes. Diagnosis rests on an occupational history and chest X-ray read by the ILO classification, with HRCT where uncertain. There is no cure: management is removal from exposure, TB screening at every visit and yearly, TB preventive treatment, symptom-guided care, and notification and social security support.

Fibrogenic mediators produce silicotic nodules and progressive massive fibrosis.
Macrophage dysfunction increases susceptibility to TB.
Fibrosis causes restrictive lung impairment and respiratory failure.
